title: A Freeze-Thawing Method to Prepare Chitosan-Poly(vinyl alcohol) Hydrogels Without Crosslinking Agents and Diflunisal Release Studies
protocol: Dissolve 0.2 g of chitosan in 10 mL of 0.1 M CH3COOH solution at room temperature and maintain continuous mechanical stirring overnight.
Dissolve 1 g of PVA in 10 mL of distilled water and stir at 80 °C for 1 h.
Mix both solutions 1:1 using a magnetic stirrer until they are homogeneous at room temperature, and pour the mixtures on Petri dishes.
Leave the samples for 2 h at atmospheric pressure to degas.
Freeze the hydrogels at -4 °C, -20 °C or -80 °C for 20 h and 4 cycles.
Freeze another hydrogel at -80 °C for 20 h using 5 or 6 freezing cycles.
After the third freezing cycle, wash the hydrogels with deionized water.
At the end, freeze-dry the hydrogels at -46 °C for 48 h and store for further characterization.
Place a little piece (1 mm x 2 mm) of hydrogel in the FT-IR spectrometer in ATR mode.
Take the FT-IR spectra from 4000 to 600 cm-1.
Cut out discs (13 mm in diameter and 10 mm in height) from the hydrogel and weigh them.
Incubate the discs in 50 mL of deionized water with shaking at 25 °C.
Repeat three times.
Remove the sample from the medium every 30 minutes.
Blot the sample to eliminate excess water.
Weigh the blotted sample.
Calculate the swelling degree using the provided equation.
Calculate the equilibrium state of swelling at 24 hours using the given equation.
Cover a small piece of hydrogel with a thin gold layer (30 seconds, 10 mA) in a sputter coater.
Place the coated sample into a scanning electron microscope (SEM).
Analyze the samples under vacuum at 20 kV and take images with magnifications of 500x and 1500x.
Prepare discs from hydrogel samples measuring approximately 15 mm in diameter and weighing around 0.26 g.
Place each disc into a penetrometer for analysis by Mercury Intrusion Porosimetry (MIP).
Conduct the experiment in hysteresis mode to measure total intrusion volume, total pore area, pore diameter, porosity, permeability, and tortuosity.
Repeat the MIP analysis twice.
Prepare samples for drug loading and release studies.
Prepare 4 L of 15 mg/L diflunisal solution and stir overnight.
Confirm the concentration of the solution by UV-Vis spectroscopy.
Swell 400 mg of freeze-dried hydrogel samples in 6 mL of distilled water for 24 hours.
Fill a flask with 50 mL of diflunisal solution and maintain at 25 °C with constant stirring.
Submerge each swelled hydrogel in the flask containing diflunisal solution.
Take aliquots (2 mL) of remaining diflunisal solution at different times: 3, 6, 24, 27, 30 and 48 hours.
Measure absorbance at 252 nm for each aliquot.
Determine the concentration of diflunisal in each aliquot using a calibration curve.
Calculate the amount of diflunisal retained in the hydrogel at 24 and 48 hours, accounting for the total volume (56 mL).
Determine the encapsulation efficiency (EE) using an appropriate equation.
Freeze the loaded hydrogels at -80 °C.
Lyophilize the frozen hydrogels at -50 °C.
Submerge 300 mg of freeze-dried diflunisal-loaded hydrogels in 50 mL of phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) at 25 °C.
Maintain constant stirring throughout the release process.
Withdraw aliquots (2 mL) at different times for analysis.
Replace withdrawn medium with fresh buffer to maintain a constant volume.
Determine the diflunisal released spectrophotometrically at 252 nm.
Adjust the drug release data corresponding to the first 60% to the Korsmeyer-Peppas model to obtain the kinetic (k) and diffusion (n) constants.
Analyze n values close to 0.5 as Fickian diffusion.
Interpret n values of 0.5-1.0 for anomalous transport involving diffusion and relaxation chains.
Consider n values of 1.0 related to case II transport.
Use the Higuchi, First order, and Zero order mathematical models to confirm results.
Select the best-fit model based on data analysis.
